title: Why GPS Alone Can't Find You Indoors for 911 #shorts
summary: Most wireless 911 calls are made indoors, where satellite location struggles (23% indoor GPS fixes in urban tests cited by the FCC); since 2015 the rules require 50 meters for 80% of calls.
sources: Dispatchable location or x/y location within 50 meters for 40% of wireless 911 calls within 2 years, 50% within 3, 70% within 5 and 80% within 6 years; the majority of wireless calls are now made indoors; satellite-based location does not give accurate location for many wireless calls; test data cited: successful indoor GPS fixes were 23 percent in urban environments (FCC Fourth Report and Order, Wireless E911 Location Accuracy Requirements, Federal Register, 4 Mar 2015): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2015-03-04/html/2015-04424.htm

Wireless 911 calls have historically been routed by the location of the cell tower that handles the call; ATIS estimates that on average 12% of wireless legacy E911 voice calls are misrouted; location-based routing is required when the caller's location is known within 165 meters at 90% confidence (nationwide carriers within 6 months, rules effective 13 May 2024); device-based hybrid location uses crowd-sourced Wi-Fi, A-GNSS and other handset sensors (FCC Report and Order, Location-Based Routing for Wireless 911 Calls, Federal Register, 13 Mar 2024): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-03-13/html/2024-03157.htm

scenes.narration: Inside city buildings, GPS got a fix just {23%|twenty-three percent} of the time, in one test the FCC cited.
And most cell calls to {911|nine one one} are now made indoors.
So in {2015|twenty fifteen}, the FCC set a new bar: within {50|fifty} meters for {80%|eighty percent} of calls.
Phones now blend satellites, nearby Wi-Fi, and their own sensors.
